If that job j starts at s > max(t, r_j), then there's idle before it. Could delaying the start of j beyond its availability ever help? Since all cost is weighted completion time and delaying the first job only delays everything or leaves subsequent jobs the same (they can't start earlier since machine busy until at least the same time... actually starting j earlier weakly decreases all subsequent completion times or leaves them unchanged), starting j at max(t,r_j) instead of later weakly improves. The key question: does the DP's restriction "start j at max(t,r_j)" lose optimality? Suppose the optimal continuation from state (R,t) starts with some job j at time s. If s > max(t, r_j), we could start j earlier at max(t,r_j), reducing its completion time and leaving more room; all other jobs' start times could be kept the same or made earlier? Actually if we start j earlier, the machine frees earlier, so subsequent jobs can only start earlier or the same (we can keep the same schedule shifted... hmm, careful). If j starts earlier and completes earlier, then all subsequent jobs in the original optimal schedule can still start at their original times (machine is free earlier), so cost weakly decreases. So WLOG the first job starts at max(t, r_j). Hence the DP is exact. Good.

But wait, there's a subtle issue: the DP state (R, t) where t is the machine-free time. But the "min over j in R of starting j at max(t,r_j)" — the claim is that any schedule is a sequence of such choices. Yes, by the argument above, any optimal continuation can be normalized so each job starts as early as possible given the previous. Hmm, actually more carefully: normalization: given an optimal schedule for the remaining jobs, consider the first started job j at time s. If s > max(t, r_j), shift j earlier to max(t,r_j). Then the rest of the schedule unchanged (jobs can still start at same times since machine is free earlier). Cost decreases by w_j*(s - max(t,r_j)) > 0. Contradiction with optimality unless... it strictly decreases, so any optimal schedule has first job starting at max(t,r_j) — wait, no: shifting j earlier decreases cost, so the original wasn't optimal. Hence optimal schedules have the first job starting at max(t, r_j). Then recurse. So the DP is exact. Good.
